title: Weekly Blog 2: What Skills Do Remote Tech Employers Actually Want?
text:
This post uses web scraping to collect 25 recent remote tech job postings from We Work Remotely and analyzes the full job descriptions to identify which technical skills appear most often.
The goal is not just to demonstrate scraping, but to answer a practical question: if you are preparing for a remote tech career, what should you learn first?

title: Weekly Blog 2: What Skills Do Remote Tech Employers Actually Want?
text:
Data Collection
I used the rvest package in R to parse the public RSS feed from We Work Remotely’s programming jobs category.

library(rvest)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(stringr)
library(purrr)
library(ggplot2)

url <- "https://weworkremotely.com/categories/remote-programming-jobs.rss"
page <- read_html(url)
items <- page %>% html_elements("item")

length(items)

[1] 25

title: Weekly Blog 2: What Skills Do Remote Tech Employers Actually Want?
text:
Data Cleaning
Each RSS <item> contains a title, region, category, publication date, and a full job description. I extracted all five fields into a tidy data frame.

titles       <- items %>% html_element("title") %>% html_text2()
regions      <- items %>% html_element("region") %>% html_text2()
categories   <- items %>% html_element("category") %>% html_text2()
dates        <- items %>% html_element("pubdate") %>% html_text2()
descriptions <- items %>% html_element("description") %>% html_text2()

jobs <- tibble(
  title       = titles,
  region      = regions,
  category    = categories,
  date        = dates,
  description = descriptions
)

glimpse(jobs)

title: Weekly Blog 2: What Skills Do Remote Tech Employers Actually Want?
text:
Analysis
I defined a list of 30 common technical skills and counted how many job descriptions mention each one. I used word-boundary regex (\\b) to avoid false matches — for example, ensuring that “Java” does not match “JavaScript”, and that “AI” does not match “email”.

skills_list <- c(
  "Python", "JavaScript", "TypeScript", "Java", "Golang",
  "React", "Vue", "Angular", "Node", "Django", "Flask",
  "SQL", "PostgreSQL", "MySQL", "MongoDB",
  "AWS", "Azure", "GCP", "Docker", "Kubernetes",
  "Git", "CI/CD", "GraphQL",
  "Machine Learning", "TensorFlow", "PyTorch",
  "HTML", "CSS", "Linux", "Bash"
)

skill_counts <- tibble(
  skill = skills_list,
  n = map_int(skills_list, function(s) {
    sum(str_detect(jobs$description,
                   regex(paste0("\\b", s, "\\b"), ignore_case = TRUE)))
  })
) |>
  filter(n > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(n))

print(skill_counts, n = 30)

skill_counts |>

  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = skill)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2c7fb8") +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), hjust = -0.3, size = 4) +
  labs(
    title = "Most In-Demand Technical Skills in Remote Jobs",
    subtitle = "Based on 25 job postings from We Work Remotely",
    x = "Number of postings mentioning this skill",
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Data source: We Work Remotely (https://weworkremotely.com)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  expand_limits(x = max(skill_counts$n) * 1.2)




Most in-demand technical skills in remote tech jobs

title: Weekly Blog 2: What Skills Do Remote Tech Employers Actually Want?
text:
Key Findings
1. Frontend frameworks lead the pack. React appears in 10 out of 25 postings (40%) — more than any other skill. This confirms that modern remote employers expect engineers to be comfortable building interactive user interfaces.
2. Cloud and DevOps skills are the new baseline. AWS (9), CI/CD (8), Docker (7), and Kubernetes (5) together appear in over 60% of postings. Cloud infrastructure and automated deployment are common expectations for remote engineers.
3. Data and database skills are expected, not optional. MongoDB (4), PostgreSQL (2), and SQL (1) appear frequently enough to confirm that remote engineers must be comfortable working with databases, even if they are not database specialists.

title: Weekly Blog 2: What Skills Do Remote Tech Employers Actually Want?
text:
Actionable Recommendation
If you are preparing for a remote tech career, prioritize:

React — it appears in 40% of postings and is the single most requested skill.
AWS + Docker + CI/CD — this trio of cloud and DevOps skills appears across more than half of the postings.
Python — the most transferable language, useful for backend, data analysis, and machine learning roles.

title: Weekly Blog 2: What Skills Do Remote Tech Employers Actually Want?
text:
Limitations
This analysis covers only 25 postings from a single RSS feed at one point in time. We Work Remotely is not representative of all remote work, and counting keywords in job descriptions is a rough proxy for skill demand.

title: Weekly Blog 2: What Skills Do Remote Tech Employers Actually Want?
text:
Data Source
All data was collected from We Work Remotely. The RSS feed is publicly available and does not require authentication.

title: Weekly Blog_Omitted variable bias
text:
Ice cream sales and drowning deaths rise together every summer. Run a simple regression of drownings on ice cream sales and the coefficient comes out “statistically significant.” The correlation between ice cream sales and drowning data is so strong that someone might argue a casual relationship from the data. But the two aren’t causing each other. They’re both driven by a third variable: hot weather. Hot days send people to the beach and to the ice cream truck at the same time. When that third variable is missing from the regression, the coefficient on the variable you did include quietly picks up its effect. That is omitted variable bias.
If weather belongs in the model naturally but the testing model omitted it, the regression has to stuff weather’s influence somewhere, and the only available place is the ice cream variable. And the error isn’t random noise — it’s a systematic bias that always points the same way. That’s why “significant” can be so misleading: the test says the pattern isn’t chance, but it says nothing about whether ice cream is the cause. The result looks like a causal relationship that isn’t there.


Make some data where weather drives both, and ice cream has nothing to do with drowning:

set.seed(1)
n <- 200

temp     <- rnorm(n, 80, 10)            # hot weather
icecream <- 5 * temp + rnorm(n, 0, 20)  # weather drives ice cream
drowning <- 2 * temp + rnorm(n, 0, 5)   # weather drives drownings

m_bad  <- lm(drowning ~ icecream)        # leave weather out
m_good <- lm(drowning ~ icecream + temp) # put weather back in

c(without_weather = coef(m_bad)["icecream"],
  with_weather    = coef(m_good)["icecream"])

without_weather.icecream    with_weather.icecream 
             0.344051514             -0.006568652 


Without weather, the ice cream coefficient is around 0.34 and looks significant — enough to write a headline about ice cream and drowning. Add weather and it drops to about zero. 0.34 was not ice cream’s strong effect to the drowning data, but was the weather’s effect hiding inside the ice cream variablee.



The same point can be written down. If the truth is \(y = \beta_1 x + \beta_2 z + u\) but you estimate \(y \sim x\), the coefficient converges to
\[\beta_1 + \beta_2\,\delta, \qquad \delta = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(x,z)}{\mathrm{Var}(x)}.\]
The bias is \(\beta_2\delta\): how strongly the omitted variable moves \(y\) (\(\beta_2\)), times how tightly it moves with the variable you kept (\(\delta\)). For ice cream, both are positive, so the number comes out too big — and you can usually tell which direction the error runs just by thinking about those two signs.



The ice cream and drowning case is obvious, but when omitted variable bias happens in real life macro data, it is somehow hard to identify. For example, the bias variable inside the testing of new medicine on certain disease. In this case, it is important and necessary to apply panel data method or use proxy variables.
